Balancing the pretreatment effect of deep eutectic solvents on biomass and the activity of β-glucosidase originating from _Paenibacillus_ sp. LLZ1
<::logo: Unknown Check for updates A square button with a red and yellow bookmark symbol within a blue circle, above the text "Check for updates".::>
Fanjin Meng , Xin Ju , Yuyang Zhou, Lishi Yan, Zhi Chen, Yuqiu Wu, Liangzhi Li *
School of Chemistry and Life Science, Suzhou University of Science and Technology, Suzhou 215009, P.R. China
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: β-Glucosidase Deep eutectic solvent Molecular docking Pretreatment

ABSTRACT The two major impediments to biomass resourcing are the catalytic efficiency of enzymes and the effectiveness of biomass pretreatment. In this study, six genes encoding β-Glucosidases (BGLs) derived from Paenibacillus sp. LLZ1 were cloned and expressed. The activity of BGL-F, which had the highest enzyme activity, was 24.1 U/mg, which was 39.8–83.7% higher than that of the other BGLs. Molecular docking and surface charge analyses showed that the binding energy of BGL-F to cellobiose and its electronegative ligand-binding pocket were greater than those of other BGLs. On the other hand, by calculating and comparing the Kamlet–Taft (KT) values of deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of different hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HDA), it was found that DES composed of betaine and glycerol had the highest α value of 0.97, meaning that it could provide the highest hydrogen bonding capacity, and thus it had the best pretreatment effect on biomass. Analysis by circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy revealed a decrease in α-helix and an increase in β-strand in the secondary structure of the DES-treated BGL-F, implying an increase in enzyme activity and stability. This result was also confirmed experimentally by the fact that the Kₘ and Vmax of the enzyme in the DES system increased by 13.2% and 57.9%, respectively, and the inactivation rate (kᵢ) decreased by 21.4%. The results of this study showed that DES consisting of glycerol-betaine achieved a better balance between the promotion of enzyme activity and biomass pretreatment.

1. Introduction With rapid economic development, people's demand for resources is increasing [1]. Among all resources, lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant and recyclable resource in nature [2]. However, since the hemicellulose and lignin in lignocellulose are wrapped around the cel- lulose by covalent and hydrogen bonds forming a tight structure [3], it is not sufficient to enhance the enzyme activity alone. Therefore, finding a way to break the hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces that form between hemicellulose and lignin, thus making it easier for enzymes to access cellulose, has become an urgent problem to solve [4]. This problem can be solved by pre-treating the biomass by deconstructing the lignified cell walls and furthering the effectiveness of the biomass con- version process [5]. Currently, research is devoted to the study of various solvents for decomposing biomass, which are not only efficient in treating biomass, but also environmentally friendly [6,7].

Among the most commonly used solvents for biomass pretreatment are ionic liquids [8–10], however, their fundamental drawbacks are their high cost and the difficulties in their dissemination and industrial

application due to the complexity of the synthesis process [11]. Recently, deep eutectic solvent (DES), a eutectic mixture of hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), has emerged as an emerging method for biomass pretreatment. DES is highly advanta- geous in biomass pre-treatment, as it is not only cost-effective, easy to synthesize, and biodegradable, but also environmentally friendly and non-combustible [12-14]. During biomass pretreatment, DES effectively separates lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose and leaves cellulose intact without severe degradation. The characteristics of the wall polymer are significantly altered during the pretreatment process, thus greatly increasing the enzymatic accessibility of cellulose [15,16]. The hydrogen bonding acidity (Kamlet-Taft α parameter) of DES is positively correlated with the effect of pretreatment [7], which elaborates the relationship between the structure and performance of DES so that the DES with the best effect of cellulose pretreatment can be rationally designed. Meanwhile, it has been reported that laccase activity can even be increased by 200 % in specific DES systems [17]. So, it is a valuable research direction to search for a DES that can enhance the enzyme activity as well as be effective for biomass pretreatment. Presently, DES

It has been demonstrated that HBD with urea-based DES improves the stability of the enzyme in the reaction system, and glycerol-based DES also promotes enzyme activity in the reaction system [21–24]. Nevertheless, studies of conformational changes of enzymes in DES systems are lacking, and investigating the reasons for the increased stability of enzymes in DES could provide further guidance for DES selection.

In this study, Paenibacillus sp. LLZ1 (P. sp. LLZ1) previously screened by our group was selected for culture [25,26], and the BGL gene from it was cloned and expressed in E. coli BL21. Differences between different genes encoding the same class of enzymes, as well as differences in the enzymatic properties of these enzymes, were studied and compared to identify and screen the enzymes with the highest enzymatic activity and stability. Specifically, the stability of the enzymes in different DES was determined. The time course of substrate hydrolysis, enzyme kinetics, and kinetics of inactivation under different DES-treated biomass were also determined. Finally, the secondary structure of the DES-treated enzyme was characterized by circular dichroism to determine the effect of DES solvent on the conformation of the enzyme. Herein, the effects of different DES on the pretreatment of biomass and enzyme activity were investigated to find the equilibrium between the two, and the effects of DES on the secondary structure of the enzyme were also investigated to elucidate the mechanism of DES-enhanced enzyme activity.
## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials _p_-nitrophenyl-β-D-glucopyranoside (_p_NPG) and _p_-Nitrophenol(_p_NP) were purchased from Aladdin (Shanghai, China). Plasmid extraction kits

and one-step PAGE gel fast preparation kits were purchased from Vazyme Biotech (Nanjing, China). BeyoGold His-tag purification resin with 50% concentration was purchased from Beyotime (Shanghai, China). Choline chloride, BTMAC, betaine, urea, glycerol, and other reagents were purchased from Aladdin (Shanghai, China).

## 2.2. Cloning of the BGL gene The whole-genome sequencing of Paenibacillus sp. LLZ1 was performed by Beijing Tsingke Biotech Co., Ltd., resulting in six genes encoding BGL. The six gene sequences were used as templates to design primers according to the primer design principle, and enzyme cleavage sites were added to the 5' and 3' ends of the primers respectively. The results of the primer design are listed in Table 1. The six genes were then amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The target genes obtained by PCR amplification were separated by 1 % agar gel electrophoresis in TAE buffer solution and purified using gel recovery for target gene isolation. The pET-22b (+) plasmid and the target gene were double cleaved with three endonucleases, EcoRI, HindIII, and BamHI. T4 ligase was used to connect the end of the target gene and the plasmid, which were cut with the same endonuclease. The final transformation into E. coli BL21 receptor cells were carried out by thermal excitation and cultured on Luria-Bertani (LB) agar plates containing 50 µg/ml of ampicillin.

2.3. Expression and purification of six BGLs The already constructed successful strain preserved in glycerol was inoculated in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium containing ampicillin. Activation was carried out by incubation at 37 °C, 200 rpm for 12–16 h. Then 1 % of the culture was inoculated in a new ampicillin-containing LB medium. At an OD600 of approximately 0.6, 0.4 mM Isopropyl β-D-Thiogalactoside (IPTG) was added to the medium, and protein expression was induced by incubation at 20 °C, 200 rpm for 20 h. The supernatant was taken and centrifuged at 4 °C, 8000 rpm for 20 min, and washed several times with PBS. Then the bacterial cell spheres were sonicated at 4 °C, and after the solution became clear and transparent, the supernatant was harvested by centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C. The Ni2+-NTA agarose gel column was used for purification. The bound recombinant protein was eluted with a gradient of imidazole solution, and then concentrated by centrifugation at 4 °C and 6000 rpm using an ultrafiltration tube and stored at 4 °C. The concentration of purified protein was determined by the Bradford method using bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a standard. The molecular weight of the enzyme and the purification process were evaluated using SDS-PAGE electrophoresis.

2.4. Enzyme assays The enzymatic activity of BGLs was measured using p-nitrophenyl-b-D-glucopyranoside (pNPG) as substrate. The previous assay protocol was continued [27]. 3 g/L (6.65 mM) pNPG and 1 g/L BGL were added to the reaction system and buffered with PBS (pH 7.0). The reaction was terminated by the addition of 1 M Na2CO3 after 1 h in a water bath shaker at 50 °C. The release of the product yield p-nitrophenyl (pNP) was determined using a colorimetric assay, and the amount of reaction product was detected at 405 nm absorbance using a 96-well plate (Sunrise; Tecan Trading AG, Männedorf, Switzerland). All data are averages of three experiments. One unit (U) of BGL activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that liberates 1 µmol pNP per minute under optimum assay conditions. The concentration of pNP was calculated from the standard curve.

2.6. DES preparation and bagasse pretreatment ChCl, btmac, and betaine as hydrogen bond acceptors and glycerol, and urea as hydrogen bond donors were heated and stirred at 80 °C for one hour. Once a clear homogeneous liquid was obtained it was cooled in a desiccator to prevent moisture absorption. The specific preparation ratios are listed in Table 2.

Using bagasse biomass as an enzymatic substrate, it needs to be pretreated using DES before in situ saccharification. Firstly, the biomass was washed three times each using anhydrous ethanol and Deionized water (DIW) respectively, dried at 55 °C, and set to constant weight. Next, the biomass for use in the reaction was obtained by pulverizing the process using a high-speed universal pulverize and passing through a 40-mesh sieve. The biomass powder was thoroughly mixed with DES and kept in a boiling water bath for 10 min until the color and fluidity of the mixed system no longer changed, and the buffer was added to cool it down to complete the pretreatment. In addition, the amounts of DES and buffer were calculated and added according to the concentration of each substance and system capacity in each experiment.

2.8. Determination of kinetic parameters The initial reaction rate of the cellulase-BGL complex enzyme preparation in the presence of different DES was determined using MCC as a substrate to determine the kinetic parameters. Vmax and Km values were calculated using Michaelis-Menten nonlinear regression.

In addition, the time-loss-of-activity kinetics of the cellulase-BGL complex enzyme preparations in different DES were determined. The residual activity (%) at certain time intervals was calculated by determining the amount of pNP produced by hydrolysis of the cellulase-BGL complex enzyme preparation at optimal pH and temperature. The initial activity at the start of the reaction was set at 100 %. The mechanics of inactivation were determined by Eq. (4)[29]. $a = (a_0 - a_p)e^{-k_d t} + a_p$ (4)

where (a), (a₀), (aₚ), and (k𝒹) denote residual activity, initial enzyme activity, final enzyme plateau activity, and equilibrium dissociation constant, respectively. In particular, (aₚ) is associated with concentration-dependent equilibrium, and both it and (k𝒹) are key data for measuring enzyme stability. High (aₚ) and low (k𝒹) indicate that the enzyme is less likely to be inactivated in the reaction system.

2.9. *Characterization* The proteins used for characterization were kept in a 25 % concentration of different DES for 12 h. The DES was then removed from the solution by dialysis and the enzyme was diluted to 0.5 g/L using ddH20 as a dispersing medium.

Circular dichroism spectra (CD spectra) were measured using a Cir- cular Dichroism Spectrometer (JASCO J-1500, JPN.) at 25 °C in the wavelength range of 180–300 nm, and the measured protein secondary structure data were analyzed using CDpro software.

LLZ1 BGLs were used as a template to obtain PCR products using _Taq_ DNA polymerase, which was transfected into _Escherichia coli_ PET-22b receptor cells after digestion and enzyme linkage. ## 3.2. Enzymatic properties of BGLs The temperature and pH dependence of the six BGLs were determined (Fig. 1), and the best performer was BGL-F. Moreover, the optimum temperature for all six BGLs was 50 °C, and the optimum pH was neutral or slightly alkaline. The specific enzyme activity of BGLs was determined at 50 °C and pH = 7, and the specific enzyme activity of BGL-F was 24.1 U/mg, which was 39.8 ~ 83.7% higher than that of the other enzymes (Fig. 2). In addition, the heat resistance of the enzyme was also explored to some extent, and it was learned that the heat resistance of BGL-F also has a great advantage compared to other enzymes (Fig. 3). To investigate the reason for the superior nature of BGL-F over other enzymes, six BGLs were molecularly docked using fiber disaccharide, the real substrate of BGL, as the substrate (Fig. 4, Fig. 5). In terms of the binding energy of the BGLs molecules to the fibrous disaccharide, the binding of all the enzymes to the substrate is an exergonic reaction, and the absolute value of the binding energy of BGL-F is the largest (Table 4) so that it achieves a more stable state than the rest of the enzymes after binding to the substrate [33]. In terms of the number of hydrogen bonds formed, BGL-F formed 2 hydrogen bonds with fiber disaccharide, which is also one of the important reasons for its stable binding state. The polarity of DESs is quantified by the Kamlet-Taft parameter, where α, β, and π* represent the offered hydrogen bonding capacity, the accepted hydrogen bonding capacity, and the polarity/polarization ratio, respectively. The α and β values of DES are closely related to the biomass pretreatment effect, with the α value being proportional to the H⁺ released during DES preparation and the β value being proportional to the number of hydrogen bonds formed [38]. Table 5 lists the α and β values of various DES with glycerol as the HBD, and it was found that the α value with betaine as the HBA was the highest. This is because betaine contains not only nitrogen ions but also carboxylic acid groups, which have strong electron-accepting and electron-giving abilities [38]. Therefore, when glycerol was used as the HBD, the DES prepared with betaine as the HBA had the best pretreatment effect.

3.4. *Enzymatic kinetic parameters in the DES system* First, we used biomass pretreated with different DESs as substrates for enzymatic hydrolysis using a cellulase-BGL combination enzyme system. The results of the experiments are shown in Fig. 7, the highest yield of glucose was obtained by enzymatic hydrolysis after DES pre- treatment prepared from glycerol-betaine. In contrast, reducing sugars

were detected in the unpretreated biomass, indicating that only a small portion of the cellulose in the biomass could be exposed to the surface of the biomass under unpretreated conditions. Similarly, in the experiment where only the biomass was pretreated without the addition of enzyme, a small portion of reducing sugar was still produced, indicating that the DES solvent has some ability to dissolve cellulose [28]. The catalytic reaction kinetics (Michaelis-Menten equation) of the cellulase-BGL complex enzyme preparation (Fig. 8A) showed that Vmax and Km were higher with increasing substrate concentration and with the presence of DES in the reaction system (Table 6). Compared to the Vmax (5.06 g/L/h) and Km (0.19 g/L) of the enzyme in PBS buffer, the enzyme had higher Vmax (5.73 g/L/h, 5.19 g/L/h) and higher Km (0.30 g/L, 0.21 g/L) with the addition of Betaine-glycerol, Btmac-glycerol. 3.5. Circular dichroism spectral characterization CD spectroscopy is an excellent technique commonly used to analyze changes in the secondary structure of proteins. The protein structure was examined at 180–300 nm and the results are shown in Table 8 and Fig. 9. In the buffer of DES prepared from betaine and glycerol, the amount of α- helix in the secondary structure of proteins decreased by 1.1 %, while the amount of β-folding increased by 1.6 %. It has been proved that the decrease in the content of α-helix and the increase in the content of β-folding will affect the active site of the enzyme, which will increase the enzyme activity [41].

In addition, the peak shape at 200–240 nm did not change after adding DES, but the signal was enhanced. It has been shown that the enhancement of signal is known to demonstrate the enhancement of protein stability. In particular, glycerol with three hydroxyl groups may bind to the protein by forming more hydrogen bonds, thus making the protein structure more rigid and stable [42].

## 4. Conclusion The P. sp. LLZ1 BGLs previously screened by our group were subjected to whole genome sequencing, and six different BGL genes originating from Bacillus-like bacteria were cloned. E. coli expressing six different BGLs were constructed on this basis. The enzyme activities of the six proteins were determined, and one of them was screened to have a relative enzyme activity of 24.1 U/mg, which was 39.8–84.7 % higher than that of the other enzymes. And its thermal stability also has a big advantage. Molecular docking of the enzyme revealed that BGL-F was the most stable in binding to the substrate. Moreover, its binding pocket consists of hydrophilic amino acids such as Glu-327 and His-321, which are more conducive to substrate binding and product generation. Charge analysis of the enzyme revealed that BGL-F has more negatively charged groups than the rest of the enzymes, and the ligand small molecules are generally bound by negatively charged pockets, which is an important reason why the activity of BGL-F is superior to that of the rest of the enzymes. Subsequently, the effect of different fractions of DES on the pretreatment of biomass and the combined enzyme system of BGL-F and

cellulase was investigated using sugarcane bagasse as substrate. By analyzing the correlation data (α, β, and π*) of DES, it was found that DES prepared when betaine was HDA and glycerol was HBD had a good pretreatment effect on biomass, which was in agreement with the experimental results. The enzymatic kinetics and inactivation mechanics parameters of the enzymes were determined and it was found that the DES solution consisting of betaine-glycerol is very biocompatible and promotes the activity of the enzymes. Finally, the DES-treated enzyme was characterized by circular dichroism spectroscopy, and it was found that the α-helix of the DES-treated enzyme was reduced and β-folding was increased. This also proved that the stability of the DES-treated enzyme was further increased.

In this study, six genes encoding β-Glucosidases (BGLs) derived from Paenibacillus sp. LLZ1 were cloned and expressed. The activity of BGL-F, which had the highest enzyme activity, was 24.1 U/mg, which was 39.8–83.7% higher than that of the other BGLs. Molecular docking and surface charge analyses showed that the binding energy of BGL-F to cellobiose and its electronegative ligand-binding pocket were greater than those of other BGLs. On the other hand, by calculating and comparing the Kamlet–Taft (KT) values of deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of different hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HDA), it was found that DES composed of betaine and glycerol had the highest α value of 0.97, meaning that it could provide the highest hydrogen bonding capacity, and thus it had the best pretreatment effect on biomass. Analysis by circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy revealed a decrease in α-helix and an increase in β-strand in the secondary structure of the DES-treated BGL-F, implying an increase in enzyme activity and stability. This result was also confirmed experimentally by the fact that the Kₘ and Vmax of the enzyme in the DES system increased by 13.2% and 57.9%, respectively, and the inactivation rate (kᵢ) decreased by 21.4%. The results of this study showed that DES consisting of glycerol-betaine achieved a better balance between the promotion of enzyme activity and biomass pretreatment. 1. Introduction With rapid economic development, people's demand for resources is increasing [1]. Among all resources, lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant and recyclable resource in nature [2]. However, since the hemicellulose and lignin in lignocellulose are wrapped around the cel- lulose by covalent and hydrogen bonds forming a tight structure [3], it is not sufficient to enhance the enzyme activity alone. Therefore, finding a way to break the hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces that form between hemicellulose and lignin, thus making it easier for enzymes to access cellulose, has become an urgent problem to solve [4]. This problem can be solved by pre-treating the biomass by deconstructing the lignified cell walls and furthering the effectiveness of the biomass con- version process [5]. Currently, research is devoted to the study of various solvents for decomposing biomass, which are not only efficient in treating biomass, but also environmentally friendly [6,7]. Among the most commonly used solvents for biomass pretreatment are ionic liquids [8–10], however, their fundamental drawbacks are their high cost and the difficulties in their dissemination and industrial application due to the complexity of the synthesis process [11]. Recently, deep eutectic solvent (DES), a eutectic mixture of hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), has emerged as an emerging method for biomass pretreatment. DES is highly advanta- geous in biomass pre-treatment, as it is not only cost-effective, easy to synthesize, and biodegradable, but also environmentally friendly and non-combustible [12-14]. During biomass pretreatment, DES effectively separates lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose and leaves cellulose intact without severe degradation. The characteristics of the wall polymer are significantly altered during the pretreatment process, thus greatly increasing the enzymatic accessibility of cellulose [15,16]. By analyzing the correlation data (α, β, and π*) of DES, it was found that DES prepared when betaine was HDA and glycerol was HBD had a good pretreatment effect on biomass, which was in agreement with the experimental results. The enzymatic kinetics and inactivation mechanics parameters of the enzymes were determined and it was found that the DES solution consisting of betaine-glycerol is very biocompatible and promotes the activity of the enzymes. Finally, the DES-treated enzyme was characterized by circular dichroism spectroscopy, and it was found that the α-helix of the DES-treated enzyme was reduced and β-folding was increased. This also proved that the stability of the DES-treated enzyme was further increased. Introduction With rapid economic development, people's demand for resources is increasing [1]. Among all resources, lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant and recyclable resource in nature [2]. However, since the hemicellulose and lignin in lignocellulose are wrapped around the cel- lulose by covalent and hydrogen bonds forming a tight structure [3], it is not sufficient to enhance the enzyme activity alone. Therefore, finding a way to break the hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces that form between hemicellulose and lignin, thus making it easier for enzymes to access cellulose, has become an urgent problem to solve [4]. This problem can be solved by pre-treating the biomass by deconstructing the lignified cell walls and furthering the effectiveness of the biomass con- version process [5]. Currently, research is devoted to the study of various solvents for decomposing biomass, which are not only efficient in treating biomass, but also environmentally friendly [6,7]. Among the most commonly used solvents for biomass pretreatment are ionic liquids [8–10], however, their fundamental drawbacks are their high cost and the difficulties in their dissemination and industrial application due to the complexity of the synthesis process [11]. Recently, deep eutectic solvent (DES), a eutectic mixture of hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), has emerged as an emerging method for biomass pretreatment. DES is highly advanta- geous in biomass pre-treatment, as it is not only cost-effective, easy to synthesize, and biodegradable, but also environmentally friendly and non-combustible [12-14]. During biomass pretreatment, DES effectively separates lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose and leaves cellulose intact without severe degradation. The characteristics of the wall polymer are significantly altered during the pretreatment process, thus greatly increasing the enzymatic accessibility of cellulose [15,16]. The hydrogen bonding acidity (Kamlet-Taft α parameter) of DES is positively correlated with the effect of pretreatment [7], which elaborates the relationship between the structure and performance of DES so that the DES with the best effect of cellulose pretreatment can be rationally designed. Meanwhile, it has been reported that laccase activity can even be increased by 200 % in specific DES systems [17]. So, it is a valuable research direction to search for a DES that can enhance the enzyme activity as well as be effective for biomass pretreatment. Presently, DES * Corresponding author. LLZ1 BGLs previously screened by our group were subjected to whole genome sequencing, and six different BGL genes originating from Bacillus-like bacteria were cloned. E. coli expressing six different BGLs were constructed on this basis. The enzyme activities of the six proteins were determined, and one of them was screened to have a relative enzyme activity of 24.1 U/mg, which was 39.8–84.7 % higher than that of the other enzymes. And its thermal stability also has a big advantage. Molecular docking of the enzyme revealed that BGL-F was the most stable in binding to the substrate. Moreover, its binding pocket consists of hydrophilic amino acids such as Glu-327 and His-321, which are more conducive to substrate binding and product generation. Charge analysis of the enzyme revealed that BGL-F has more negatively charged groups than the rest of the enzymes, and the ligand small molecules are generally bound by negatively charged pockets, which is an important reason why the activity of BGL-F is superior to that of the rest of the enzymes. Subsequently, the effect of different fractions of DES on the pretreatment of biomass and the combined enzyme system of BGL-F and cellulase was investigated using sugarcane bagasse as substrate. By analyzing the correlation data (α, β, and π*) of DES, it was found that DES prepared when betaine was HDA and glycerol was HBD had a good pretreatment effect on biomass, which was in agreement with the experimental results. The enzymatic kinetics and inactivation mechanics parameters of the enzymes were determined and it was found that the DES solution consisting of betaine-glycerol is very biocompatible and promotes the activity of the enzymes.
